topic.title: What holds up the Burj Khalifa: a concrete raft, salty groundwater, and 192 bored piles reaching more than 50 m down

title: What's Under the Burj Khalifa?
description:
What's under the Burj Khalifa?
Under the world's tallest building sit a concrete raft, salty groundwater and a forest of bored concrete piles.
Sources: Wikipedia (2025).
Depths from published sources. Cutaway illustrations, not to scale.
cta: Tallest tower or deepest station: what should we dive under next? Comment

lines.text: The Burj Khalifa is the tallest tower on Earth. So what's underneath it?
A giant concrete slab carries the whole tower.
Below it, salty groundwater that eats concrete. So how does it stand?
So 192 concrete piles, each 43 m long, are drilled down through it.
Their tips sit more than 50 m below the street.
The foundation alone weighs more than 110,000 tonnes.
All of it, holding up the Burj Khalifa.

Beat 'piles': 'are driven down through it' is wrong engineering. The Burj Khalifa piles are bored (drilled and cast in place) piles: the topic itself says '192 bored piles', and Poulos & Bunce (ISSMGE 2008), as summarised in several design write-ups, describes 'bored piles, 1.5 m diameter'. Driven piles are hammered in, which is a different method. Fix: say 'are drilled down through it' (or 'bored'), and change the 'driven' moment ('they drive down to their full length') to drilling. Everything else checks out: Wikipedia (fetched) shows 192 piles, 1.5 m by 43 m, 'buried more than 50 m (164 ft) deep', 'more than 110,000 tonnes' of concrete, and sulphate- and chloride-rich groundwater under a cathodic protection system. The description ends with the channel disclaimer. Note: other sources give 194 piles and 47.45 m; the script follows Wikipedia, its named source, which is acceptable.

[scene] 0.0s, 23.5s and thumbnail (Dive surface preset 'tower'): the Burj Khalifa is drawn as a generic boxy mid-rise block with a square window grid, not the stepped needle, so only the grey label says what it is. The raft slab is drawn above the street, in front of the taxis, and cuts the bottom off the 'BURJ KHALIFA' label. A stray 'RAFT' label already shows at the bottom of 0.0s, before the raft beat, and at 23.5s it is clipped ('R  FT') by the frame edge.

[script] 5.0s (raft beat): a plain grey rectangle floats in bare sand. About 60% of the frame is empty sand with the 'RAFT' label alone in the middle, away from the slab. Nothing is poured, nothing presses down, nothing moves. The meter's '4 m / 14 ft below' comes from the director's ft:14, which is in neither the facts nor the line, so it is a figure typed by an LLM (the same problem rejected on v-20261121-52). Source it or hide the meter on that layer.

[script] 10.0s and 20.0s (check D): 192 and 110,000 are shown as floating black headline cards over the piles instead of on a thing in the place (a sign, a stamp, a tag, like v-20261121-53's station signs). At 10.0s the 'Data: Wikipedia · 2025' chip overlaps the top of the PILES card. At 20.0s the 'FOUNDATION WEIGHT · TONNES' label is wider than its card: the F and the S run past its edges. A tiny unreadable stamp strip also crosses the piles at the waterline.

[script] 15.0s (tips beat): the piles stop around mid-frame, but the 'PILE TIPS · 50 M' ring, flag and tag sit far below them in bare brown soil, so the tips are not where the tag says. The bottom half is empty striped soil. The same gap shows on the 20.0s pull-back, where the ring floats well below the pile ends. The meter also reads 46 m at 10.0s for 43 m piles under a raft whose depth isn't sourced.

[scene] Weaker than our best, v-20261121-53: its every still has trains or riders moving through lit places. Here 5.0s, 10.0s and 15.0s are bare sand or striped soil with a few grey bars and nothing in motion: no rig, no workers, no water visibly attacking concrete. Give each layer a built, busy set (a pour or a rig at the raft, a pile-driving rig, corrosion on the concrete).

[script] Story notes from the number check still stand: 0 beats between the hook and the payoff open a new question (at least 2), and only 2 build beats. The 6.5-9 s groundwater beat falls between stills and was not judged.
